pharm: Taxane; microtubule-stabilizing mitotic inhibitor (solvent-based, polyoxyl 35 castor oil formulation)
quick: IV: 135-175 mg/m2 over 3 or 24 h per cycle (regimen-specific)
Can cause fetal harm; avoid; advise effective contraception
Effect of renal impairment not studied; clearance mainly non-renal
Reduce dose; higher myelosuppression risk (see TABLE 17)
Vehicle contains 396 mg/mL ethanol; consider CNS effects
Frequent CBC, vital signs during infusion, hypersensitivity
summary: Paclitaxel is a taxane antineoplastic that promotes assembly of microtubules and prevents their depolymerization, arresting cell division. It is given by IV infusion to treat advanced ovarian carcinoma, node-positive and metastatic breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, and AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma. It carries a BOXED WARNING for two life-threatening risks: severe hypersensitivity/anaphylactic reactions (occurring in 2-4% of patients and sometimes fatal despite premedication, so all patients must be pretreated with a corticosteroid, diphenhydramine, and an H2 antagonist, and patients with severe reactions must not be rechallenged) and severe dose-limiting bone marrow suppression, primarily neutropenia (do not give to solid-tumor patients with baseline neutrophils <1,500 cells/mm3, or to Kaposi's sarcoma patients with <1,000 cells/mm3, and monitor blood counts frequently). It must be administered only under supervision of a physician experienced in cancer chemotherapy with facilities for managing complications.
indications: Advanced carcinoma of the ovary - subsequent therapy, or first-line in combination with cisplatin
Adjuvant treatment of node-positive breast cancer, given sequentially to standard doxorubicin-containing combination chemotherapy

Breast cancer after failure of combination chemotherapy for metastatic disease or relapse within 6 months of adjuvant chemotherapy (prior therapy should have included an anthracycline unless contraindicated)
First-line treatment of non-small cell lung cancer, in combination with cisplatin, in patients who are not candidates for potentially curative surgery and/or radiation
Second-line treatment of AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma

dosage.d: Paclitaxel 175 mg/m2 over 3 h followed by cisplatin 75 mg/m2; OR paclitaxel 135 mg/m2 over 24 h followed by cisplatin 75 mg/m2
dosage.n: Select regimen considering differences in toxicities; premedicate before every dose

dosage.d: Paclitaxel 135 mg/m2 or 175 mg/m2 over 3 h
dosage.n: Optimal regimen not yet clear; several doses/schedules have been used
Administered sequentially to doxorubicin-containing combination chemotherapy (trial used 4 courses of doxorubicin plus cyclophosphamide)

dosage.c: Breast cancer - after chemotherapy failure / relapse
dosage.n: After failure of initial chemotherapy for metastatic disease or relapse within 6 months of adjuvant therapy

dosage.d: Paclitaxel 135 mg/m2 over 24 h followed by cisplatin 75 mg/m2
dosage.n: For patients not candidates for curative surgery and/or radiation

dosage.d: Paclitaxel 135 mg/m2 over 3 h every 3 weeks; OR 100 mg/m2 over 3 h every 2 weeks (dose intensity 45-50 mg/m2/week)
dosage.n: 135 mg/m2 q3wk was more toxic; reduce premedication dexamethasone to 10 mg PO; only initiate/repeat if neutrophils >=1,000 cells/mm3; reduce subsequent doses 20% for severe neutropenia; add G-CSF as clinically indicated

dosage.c: Dose modification - severe neutropenia or neuropathy
dosage.d: Reduce dose by 20% for subsequent courses
dosage.n: For neutrophils <500 cells/mm3 for >=1 week, or severe peripheral neuropathy; neurotoxicity and neutropenia severity increase with dose

dosage.d: Do not repeat course until neutrophils >=1,500 cells/mm3 and platelets >=100,000 cells/mm3
dosage.n: For KS, do not give if baseline or subsequent neutrophils <1,000 cells/mm3

admin: PREMEDICATE all patients before every dose to prevent severe hypersensitivity: dexamethasone 20 mg PO at approximately 12 h and 6 h before paclitaxel; diphenhydramine (or equivalent) 50 mg IV 30-60 min before; and cimetidine 300 mg or ranitidine 50 mg IV 30-60 min before (reduce dexamethasone to 10 mg PO in advanced HIV/KS patients)
Dilute before use; administer through an in-line filter with a microporous membrane not greater than 0.22 microns

Avoid contact of undiluted concentrate with plasticized PVC equipment; store diluted solution in glass, polypropylene, or polyolefin containers and give through polyethylene-lined administration sets to limit DEHP plasticizer leaching
Cytotoxic drug - handle with gloves; if solution contacts skin wash immediately with soap and water; flush mucous membranes thoroughly with water
Monitor vital signs frequently, particularly during the first hour of infusion; continuous cardiac monitoring is not routinely required except in patients with serious conduction abnormalities

Minor symptoms (flushing, skin reactions, mild dyspnea, hypotension, tachycardia) do not require interruption; severe reactions (hypotension needing treatment, dyspnea needing bronchodilators, angioedema, generalized urticaria) require immediate discontinuation and aggressive symptomatic therapy - do not rechallenge
moa: Paclitaxel is an antimicrotubule agent that promotes assembly of microtubules from tubulin dimers and stabilizes them by preventing depolymerization. This stabilization inhibits the normal dynamic reorganization of the microtubule network required for vital interphase and mitotic functions, and induces abnormal microtubule bundles throughout the cell cycle and multiple asters during mitosis, thereby arresting cell division and producing cytotoxicity.

absolute: History of hypersensitivity reactions to paclitaxel or to other drugs formulated in polyoxyl 35 castor oil (e.g., cyclosporine injection concentrate, teniposide injection concentrate)
Solid tumors with baseline neutrophil count <1,500 cells/mm3 (boxed warning)
AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma with baseline neutrophil count <1,000 cells/mm3 (boxed warning)
relative: Prior severe hypersensitivity reaction to paclitaxel - do not rechallenge (boxed warning)
Hepatic impairment (increased toxicity, especially grade III-IV myelosuppression; reduce dose)
Concomitant CYP2C8/CYP3A4 substrates, inhibitors, or inducers
monitor: Frequent peripheral blood cell counts (neutrophils, platelets) - boxed warning for severe marrow suppression
Signs of hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis during infusion - boxed warning
Vital signs, especially first hour of infusion (hypotension, bradycardia, hypertension)
Cardiac conduction in patients with conduction abnormalities; cardiac function when combined with doxorubicin

preg: Can cause fetal harm. In rabbits, paclitaxel during organogenesis at 3 mg/kg/day (about 0.2 times the daily maximum recommended human dose on a mg/m2 basis) caused embryo- and fetotoxicity (intrauterine mortality, increased resorptions and fetal deaths) plus maternal toxicity; teratogenic potential could not be assessed at higher doses due to extensive fetal mortality. No adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. If used in pregnancy, or if the patient becomes pregnant, apprise her of the potential hazard to the fetus. Women of childbearing potential should avoid becoming pregnant.
lact: It is not known whether paclitaxel is excreted in human milk. In lactating rats, radioactivity concentrations in milk exceeded those in plasma. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, discontinue nursing during paclitaxel therapy.
renal: The effect of renal dysfunction on paclitaxel disposition has not been investigated. Paclitaxel undergoes extensive non-renal (hepatic/biliary) clearance, with only about 1.3% to 12.6% of a dose recovered unchanged in urine; no specific renal dose adjustment is provided in the label.
hepatic: Patients with hepatic impairment are at increased risk of toxicity, particularly grade III-IV myelosuppression. The label provides first-course dose recommendations for both 3- and 24-hour infusions in hepatic impairment (TABLE 17), with further reduction in later courses based on individual tolerance. Plasma exposure is increased with abnormal bilirubin up to 2x ULN; patients with total bilirubin >2x ULN had a higher incidence of severe myelosuppression even at a reduced dose (110 mg/m2). Exercise extreme caution and monitor closely for profound myelosuppression.

major: Cisplatin - giving paclitaxel AFTER cisplatin causes more profound myelosuppression and decreases paclitaxel clearance by approximately 33% (administer paclitaxel before cisplatin)
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (atazanavir, clarithromycin, indinavir, itraconazole, ketoconazole, nefazodone, nelfinavir, ritonavir, saquinavir, telithromycin) - may increase paclitaxel exposure
CYP2C8 inhibitor gemfibrozil - may increase paclitaxel exposure
Doxorubicin - plasma levels of doxorubicin and its active metabolite doxorubicinol may be increased in combination
moderate: CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine) - may decrease paclitaxel exposure
CYP2C8 inducer rifampin - may decrease paclitaxel exposure
CYP3A4 substrates (midazolam, buspirone, felodipine, lovastatin, eletriptan, sildenafil, simvastatin, triazolam) - exercise caution
minor: Protease inhibitors (ritonavir, saquinavir, indinavir, nelfinavir) - potential CYP3A4 interactions not evaluated in clinical trials
interactions.alcohol: The paclitaxel vehicle contains dehydrated alcohol USP, 396 mg/mL; consideration should be given to possible CNS and other effects of alcohol, and overdose in pediatric patients may be associated with acute ethanol toxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: Bone marrow suppression appears as neutropenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia on CBC; reversible elevations of bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and AST (SGOT) and abnormal ECGs may occur.

serious: Severe neutropenia (nadir about day 11) with risk of life-threatening infection - dose-limiting (boxed warning)
rare: Severe cardiac conduction abnormalities (<1%, occasionally requiring pacemaker)
Injection site reactions including extravasation injury
emergency: Anaphylaxis / severe hypersensitivity reaction - dyspnea and hypotension requiring treatment, angioedema, generalized urticaria; occurs in 2-4% and can be fatal despite premedication (boxed warning) - stop infusion immediately, give aggressive symptomatic therapy, do NOT rechallenge

monitoring: Frequent peripheral blood cell counts in all patients (boxed warning - monitor for severe neutropenia/marrow suppression)
Signs and symptoms of hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis during and after infusion (boxed warning)
Vital signs frequently, particularly during the first hour of infusion
Verify retreatment criteria before each cycle (neutrophils >=1,500/mm3 and platelets >=100,000/mm3; >=1,000/mm3 for KS)
Cardiac monitoring in patients with conduction abnormalities; cardiac function when used with doxorubicin
Liver function tests (bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, AST)
counsel: This medicine is given by infusion in a clinic or hospital; you will receive premedication beforehand to reduce the risk of a severe allergic reaction
Tell staff at once during the infusion about flushing, rash, trouble breathing, chest tightness, dizziness, or swelling - these can signal a serious allergic reaction
Report fever, chills, sore throat, or any sign of infection promptly because your white blood cells may be very low
Report unusual bruising or bleeding (low platelets)
Numbness, tingling, or burning in the hands and feet (peripheral neuropathy) is common - report it, as the dose may need to be reduced
Hair loss is common and is usually reversible after treatment ends
Avoid becoming pregnant during treatment; the drug can harm an unborn baby, and nursing should be stopped during therapy
The infusion contains alcohol, which may rarely cause drowsiness or other effects
pk: Immediate (IV); antimitotic effect within the cell cycle
End of infusion; Cmax ~2,170-3,650 ng/mL (3-h infusions of 135-175 mg/m2)
Terminal t-half about 13-52 h (varies with dose and infusion duration)
Neutrophil nadir at median ~11 days; recovery before next 2-3 week cycle
Store vials in original carton at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light
pearls: BOXED WARNING #1 - severe hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (2-4%, can be fatal despite premedication): ALWAYS premedicate with a corticosteroid, diphenhydramine, and an H2 antagonist, and never rechallenge after a severe reaction
BOXED WARNING #2 - severe dose-limiting neutropenia: do NOT give to solid-tumor patients with baseline neutrophils <1,500/mm3 (or KS patients <1,000/mm3); monitor blood counts frequently
Hypersensitivity is largely attributed to the polyoxyl 35 castor oil (Cremophor EL) vehicle; cross-reacts with other castor-oil-formulated drugs
Sequence matters with platinum: give paclitaxel BEFORE cisplatin - the reverse sequence worsens myelosuppression and cuts paclitaxel clearance ~33%
Metabolized by CYP2C8 (major, to 6-alpha-hydroxypaclitaxel) and CYP3A4; watch for interactions with inhibitors/inducers of these enzymes
Must be administered only under supervision of a physician experienced in cancer chemotherapy with adequate facilities to manage complications
missed: Paclitaxel is given as a scheduled IV infusion in cycles, not as a take-home dose. If a scheduled infusion or cycle is missed or delayed, contact the oncology team promptly so they can reassess blood counts and reschedule; courses are not repeated until neutrophils recover to >=1,500 cells/mm3 (>=1,000 for Kaposi's sarcoma) and platelets to >=100,000 cells/mm3. Do not attempt to make up or double a dose.
overdose: There is no known antidote. The primary anticipated complications of overdosage are bone marrow suppression, peripheral neurotoxicity, and mucositis. Overdoses in pediatric patients may be associated with acute ethanol toxicity from the alcohol-containing vehicle. Management is supportive, including monitoring and treatment of myelosuppression (with hematopoietic support and infection management as needed).
